title: Water Promised to the Thirsty
english: …God says that He Himself is, and He leads them to consider that they ought to honor Him, as the one who has become the giver of their very being and the cause of existence to those who once were not. And by saying to those who have sinned, “You will still be helped” (Isaiah 44:2), He gives them courage: although they are caught in many charges they cannot escape, a remnant of gentleness and love for humankind has been kept for them. Nothing would keep them, too, from being saved, if they chose to pass over to what is better and more fitting and in keeping with the laws He gave.

“Fear not, my servant Jacob, and beloved Israel, whom I have chosen. For I will give water in thirst to those who walk in a waterless land. I will put My Spirit upon your seed, and My blessings upon your children. And they will spring up like grass among the waters, and like a willow beside flowing water. This one will say, ‘I am God’s,’ and that one will cry out in the name of Jacob; and another will write, ‘I am God’s,’ in the name of Israel” (Isaiah 44:2-5).

Here he seems to call the company of the holy apostles Israel and Jacob, understood as a single person; for all are one in Christ (Galatians 3:28). See how he says that this Israel is beloved and chosen; and surely it is plain to all that He would never have called those who had rejected faith in Him beloved and chosen. But since, being of the blood of Jacob, who is also Israel, they became precious and chosen vessels and were called to the sacred service of the gospel preaching, He thought it right to crown them with words so splendid, since they were to be like lights in the world, holding fast the word of life (Philippians 2:15-16), and guides into the mystery for all that lies under the sun.

“Fear not,” then, he says; that is: be of good courage and be strong, keep a mind that endures hardship and is full of vigor, laugh at the assaults of those who persecute you, and hold your faith in God firm. For a great many fight against the sacred preaching, and an unholy multitude will rise up against you, working against the words you speak. But be stronger than fear, he says, than hesitation and faint-heartedness. For “I will give water to those who walk in a waterless land” (Isaiah 44:3).

For those who walk through a thirsty land it is sweet and life-saving to come upon springs of water. And for those who labor for the sake of godliness, we say, it is still more longed for to be watered by divine and spiritual streams, that is, by the comforts given through the Spirit, by which the human mind, when it has somehow grown faint, may soon be strengthened again for courage. The water here, which God promises to supply to those who walk in a waterless land, we say is the Holy Spirit. Indeed the Savior Himself said: “As the Scripture has said, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7:38). And making plain the force of these words, the all-wise …

title: The Foundations of the Earth Sound the Trumpet
english: …the whole earth to the knowledge of the truth, as Christ was bringing it back, calling it to conversion, justifying it by faith, and making it glorious through sanctification, there was joy and festival among the spirits above. So while the heavens rejoiced because God had mercy on Israel (Isaiah 44:23), and not only on Israel according to the flesh but also on the Israel understood according to the spirit, the foundations of the earth sounded the trumpet, that is, those who perform the sacred service of the gospel oracles. Their piercing sound was carried everywhere, and like sacred trumpets they cried aloud, proclaiming the Savior’s glory to people everywhere and calling to the knowledge of Christ both those of the circumcision and those who once worshiped the creation rather than the Creator (Romans 1:25).

For what reason do we say they are called the foundations of the earth? Christ is indeed the foundation of all and the unshakable base, who upholds all things and holds firm in well-being whatever has been set upon Him. For on Him we are all built up, a spiritual house (1 Peter 2:5), fitted together through the Spirit into a holy temple, into His dwelling place (Ephesians 2:20-22). For He dwells in our hearts through faith (Ephesians 3:17). But the apostles and evangelists may be understood as foundations nearer to Him and closer than we are, since they became eyewitnesses and ministers of the word (Luke 1:2), and became also a firm support for the faith. For when we recognize that we must follow their traditions, we shall keep our faith in Christ straight and undistorted.

For somewhere He said to the godly Peter, when Peter was wisely and blamelessly confessing his faith in Him and saying, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16:16): “You are Peter, and on this rock I will found My Church” (Matthew 16:18). By the rock, I think, He means the disciple’s unshakable firmness in faith. It is also said somewhere through the voice of the Psalmist: “His foundations are in the holy mountains” (Psalm 87:1). The holy apostles and evangelists may very fitly be compared to holy mountains; their knowledge has been laid like a foundation for those who came after them, and it does not let those whom they gathered in their net fall away into what is counterfeit in faith.

So the foundations of the earth sound the trumpet. But notice the exactness of the words. Moses was weak of voice and slow of tongue (Exodus 4:10), for the Law could be heard only by those in Judea. But sound the trumpet, you who are ambassadors for Christ (2 Corinthians 5:20)! “For their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 19:4; Romans 10:18). He has commanded the mountains to shout for joy (Isaiah 44:23), here again calling the foundations of the earth mountains. For the godly disciples are admired and conspicuous, distinguished in deed and word, and to people everywhere …

title: Mercy from the Earth and Man Formed from Clay
english: …and arbiter and teacher, Christ Himself has become for us. One might also say that the mercy and righteousness that rises from the earth, or springs up from it (Isaiah 45:8), is our Lord Jesus Christ Himself. For He has become for us, from God the Father, mercy and righteousness (compare 1 Corinthians 1:30), since it is true that in Him we received mercy and were justified, receiving forgiveness of our old offenses; that is, from Him we have received the righteousness that can bring us to our share in every good, the righteousness by which we have also been saved.

If the earth is commanded to make righteousness spring up, let no one be annoyed, when he considers that the Psalmist too says somewhere, of God the Father and of Emmanuel Himself: “He worked righteousness in the midst of the earth” (Psalm 74:12). For Christ did not bring His own flesh down to us from above, out of heaven; rather, He was born according to the flesh of a woman (Galatians 4:4), who was herself one of those on the earth. So when He is said to have become the fruit and shoot of the earth, you will understand, as I said, that He was born according to the flesh of a woman taken for this service, though she was one of those from the earth.
“I am the Lord God, who created you. What better thing have I made, like a potter’s clay?” (Isaiah 45:8-9).

Here He gives, as it were, the reason why the Son, though He is God by nature, emptied Himself, chose even to suffer for us, and counted those on the earth worthy of so great a care that He gave up His own life in exchange for them; or rather, why He consented to take the form of a servant (Philippians 2:7) and to exchange the supreme glory for the lowliness of human nature. That is why He says, “I am”; this is to be taken here in place of “I subsist and live,” since He is true God and Lord of hosts, who brought all things into being, who did not make death but rather created all things for incorruption (Wisdom of Solomon 1:13-14; 2:23).

Then, honoring human nature, and showing that of all living creatures on earth none at all could match it, He says, “What better thing have I made, like a potter’s clay?” For we were formed by Him when He took dust from the earth (Genesis 2:7) and shaped it very well, as a potter does. Yet the dignity of human nature does not stop there; there is in us something greater still, a guest-gift and a present from God’s fine craftsmanship. For we have been made according to His image and likeness (Genesis 1:26), and we have been enriched with the stamp of His glory, shining spiritually in our souls, even though according to the flesh we are earth and from the earth.

So man is no contemptible creature, but rather a living being on earth worthy of admiration; and God takes such pride in him. Indeed He said to Job, who endured so much, when He was setting out His mighty works plainly: “Did you take clay of the earth and form a living creature, and set it on the earth able to speak?” (Job 38:14) …
